questions.specialNote: The printed options contain no general necessary condition. The GATE Overflow variant of B uses min, which gives the necessary bound for at least one remaining request to proceed.
questions.reason: With holdings (1, 1, 2, 1) and requests (0, 0, 1, 3), p and q free two units. The third process can finish and raise the free count to four, enabling the last process even though B fails. This also refutes C and D. A fails for holdings (2, 2, 1, 1) and requests (0, 0, 1, 1), where all processes finish.
questions.note: The app, Made Easy and linked paper use max in B. Use x_p + x_q >= min_{k != p,q} y_k for the necessary condition for further progress after p and q finish. GATE Overflow also has max(x_p, x_q) > 1 in C, where the app has min(x_p, x_q) < 1. The linked paper's reference explanation confirms that none of its listed choices is correct.

questions.specialNote: Specify that each process can hold at most two units at once and may acquire them one at a time. Replace D (4) with D (6), the minimum process count that allows deadlock.
questions.reason: With a maximum demand of two units, each deadlocked process can hold at most one. Exhausting six units needs at least six such holders. Six processes can each hold one and wait for another, so none of the listed values works.
questions.note: The archived official answer sheet and GATE Overflow key D (4). Made Easy prints an asterisk without a legend. The equivalent six-drive problem at Q2 confirms that up to five processes are safe under the same maximum-demand model.
